label: Projective Geometry
notes: This chapter spans printed pages 393 through 476 and completes affine geometry by adding points at infinity. Projective space makes intersection theory uniform: parallel lines meet, conics and lines always intersect in the expected number of points, and many theorems take their cleanest form here.

label: Projective Space
notes: Projective space consists of lines through the origin in one higher dimension, recorded by homogeneous coordinates determined up to a common nonzero scalar. The affine space embeds as a dense open set, and its complement, the hyperplane at infinity, captures asymptotic directions of affine objects.

label: Homogeneous Ideals
notes: Projective varieties are defined by homogeneous polynomials, those whose terms all share one degree, since vanishing must be independent of the chosen scalar. The ideals generated by homogeneous polynomials are homogeneous ideals, and the dictionary between varieties and ideals carries over with this grading.

label: Homogenization
notes: Homogenizing an affine polynomial by inserting an extra variable produces its projective closure, while setting that variable to one dehomogenizes back. These operations move freely between affine and projective views, with a homogenizing Grobner basis computing the projective closure of an affine variety.

label: Bezout's Theorem
notes: In the projective plane two curves of degrees m and n meet in exactly m times n points, counted with multiplicity and over an algebraically closed field. Bezout's theorem epitomizes the clean intersection theory that motivates the projective viewpoint and underlies the study of plane curves.

label: Projective Elimination
notes: Elimination in the projective setting needs the multivariable resultant and a projective Extension Theorem, since points at infinity can absorb missing solutions. With these the algorithmic toolkit extends to projective varieties, closing the geometric core. Next: the dimension of a variety.
